outcomes.original: Expected condition: Operating hours limited to close by 10 pm or 11 pm, consistent with the Youth and Family SUD's intent to reduce late-night impacts near residential uses. Basis: The SoMa Youth and Family SUD was adopted to protect residential character and youth-serving uses. The one CUA in the SUD (2018-004720CUA) for a restaurant with alcohol had no late-night flag in the data, and Planning Code Section 249.40A lists conditional-use findings focused on residential compatibility. MUR districts typically have no hours control, so hours limits come from SUD discretionary review.
outcomes.note: Records confirm the CUA had no late-night flag but do not state the SUD's purpose, Section 249.40A content, MUR hours rules, or that hours limits come from SUD review.

outcomes.original: Expected condition: Adoption of a written good-neighbor policy under Planning Code Section 803.5, addressing noise, litter, queuing and community liaison. Basis: A 2015 agency referral at 917 Folsom (2015-005755MIS) for continuation of a nightclub use was conditioned to 'operate in conformance with Good Neighbor Policies per Section 803.5.' Although that was a nightclub, Section 803.5 applies to any eating and drinking establishment, and the Commission routinely imposes good-neighbor policies on CUAs in residential-adjacent districts.

outcomes.original: Expected condition: Compliance with any noise and odor mitigation measures required by DPH and DBI, including hood and exhaust system sizing and operation to minimize impacts on residential units above or adjacent. Basis: Limited cooking is proposed; DPH plan check will classify the facility and require a Type I or Type II hood. The Youth and Family SUD CU findings include compatibility with surrounding uses, so the Commission will condition the CUA on compliance with DPH ventilation and noise standards, especially if residential units are nearby.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Schedule a pre-application meeting with San Francisco Planning Department to confirm the CU pathway, SUD requirements and whether the limited-restaurant use is considered active. What to say: Present the concept as a 1,800 sq ft restaurant with limited cooking (no full commercial kitchen), no alcohol and occupancy under 50, operating in a space last used as a limited restaurant. Ask whether the Youth and Family SUD's CU requirement applies if the use is a continuation rather than a new establishment, and whether formula-retail review is triggered if the business is independent. Request confirmation of the Section 311 neighborhood-notice requirement and whether the change from limited to full restaurant triggers it. Ask for guidance on likely conditions (hours, good-neighbor policy, noise) and whether any fee waivers apply under the Priority Equity Geographies SUD.
outcomes.note: The records confirm the two SUDs apply at the address but state their restaurant permissions are 'unknown' and do not describe any CU requirements, Section 311 notices, fee waivers, or conditions.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the Conditional Use Authorization application with San Francisco Planning under Planning Code Section 303, with the application fee (estimated $3,100 for a no-construction CU in 2023), project description, floor plan, proposed hours and a draft good-neighbor policy. What to say: Frame the restaurant as compatible with the Youth and Family SUD's goals: a neighborhood-serving, affordable dining option with limited cooking, no alcohol and early closing hours that will not generate late-night noise or loitering. Emphasize the immediate block's established restaurant character (active uses at 915-917 Folsom with ABC licenses) and the lack of late-night entertainment or bar use. Commit to a written good-neighbor policy under Section 803.5, including a community liaison, litter and noise management, and no outdoor amplified sound. If the business is independent and local, state that it is not formula retail. Request that the CU be processed concurrently with the health plan check and building permit referrals to shorten the overall timeline.
outcomes.note: The records do not state the code sections, fee amount, SUD goals, nearby uses, good-neighbor policy requirement, or concurrent processing procedure.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Submit the DPH plan check application (estimated $828–$2,207 for 2023) with scaled drawings, equipment layout, menu and finishes schedule, and note that the CU application is pending. What to say: Submit two sets of plans showing the kitchen layout, hand sinks, prep surfaces, storage, restrooms and the proposed cooking equipment (if limited to rapid-cook ovens, microwaves and griddles, specify that to avoid a Type I hood requirement). Describe the menu and food handling: for example, 'limited menu of reheated, grilled and assembled items; no deep frying, no char-grilling.' Request that DPH route the referral to Planning in parallel with the CU review so that final health permit issuance can occur immediately after CU approval. Confirm the FOG discharger category and grease-interceptor requirement with the plan reviewer.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the building permit application with DBI for tenant improvements, including architectural plans stamped by a licensed architect, and list Planning as a routing department for the change-of-use review. What to say: Submit plans showing the existing layout, proposed TI work (partitions, finishes, MEP upgrades, ADA compliance), occupant load calculation (under 50 for Group B occupancy) and a narrative stating 'Change of use from limited restaurant to restaurant; Conditional Use Authorization application filed with Planning under case number [CUA case number].' Request that DBI hold issuance pending Planning's CU approval and DPH's final health inspection. If a grease interceptor is required, include it in the plumbing plans and coordinate sizing with SFPUC's FOG program before submitting.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Attend the Planning Commission hearing (typically 4–8 months after filing the CU application), present the project and respond to Commissioner questions and any public comment. What to say: Reiterate the project's fit with the Youth and Family SUD: a daytime and early-evening restaurant serving affordable prepared meals, no alcohol, no late-night hours, in a block that already has restaurant uses. Highlight the good-neighbor commitments: hours ending by 10 pm (or whatever Planning recommends), a community liaison contact, regular sidewalk cleaning and no outdoor amplified music. If neighbors or youth-serving organizations are present, acknowledge their concerns and offer to meet regularly. Accept any reasonable conditions the Commission proposes on hours, noise or operations. After the hearing, if the CU is approved, the 30-day appeal period begins; if appealed to the Board of Supervisors, budget another 2–3 months.
outcomes.note: Records show one CU case timeline but do not state what is typical; do not show restaurant uses on the block; do not state appeal periods.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Once the CU is approved and the appeal period expires (or any appeal is resolved), request that DBI and DPH complete their referral reviews and issue the building permit and health permit to operate. What to say: Notify DBI and DPH that the CU authorization is final (provide the motion number and effective date). Request that DBI schedule the final building inspection and that DPH schedule the pre-opening health inspection. Confirm that a certified food protection manager is on staff (required within 60 days of opening) and that all employees will obtain California food handler cards within 30 days of hire. Have proof of workers' compensation insurance and the San Francisco business registration certificate on hand for the inspectors.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Complete pre-opening tasks: obtain ASCAP and BMI music licenses (1–7 days, $300–$2,500 each annually), arrange organics recycling service under SB 1383, and post the health permit and occupancy placard. What to say: Register online with ASCAP and BMI for public performance of recorded music (required for background music in a dining room). Subscribe to a licensed organics hauler for green-bin service (required for any commercial food business under SB 1383; coordinate with the existing refuse hauler). Display the DPH permit to operate, the DBI occupancy placard and the business registration certificate in public view. Keep on file the CU motion, the building permit sign-off, proof of workers' comp insurance and food safety certifications for inspectors.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 135 to 345 days. Estimated government cost: $5,173 to $21,350. Notes: The timeline is 135–345 days and the cost is $5,200–$21,400 to obtain the three approvals in the entitlement path: Conditional Use Authorization, health permit to operate and building permit with change of use. These are the days to approval when the approvals are granted, not to a denial or withdrawal. The timeline counts from filing the CU application to final issuance of the health permit and building permit, which cannot occur until after the CU is approved and any appeal period expires. The one comparable CUA for a restaurant in the Youth and Family SUD took 229 days from filing to approval (April to November 2018); budget 4–8 months for CU review, hearing, adoption and appeal period, then 2–4 months for concurrent building permit and health permit plan check, inspections and final issuance. Costs: CU application fee ~$3,100 (2023 estimate); health plan check $828–$2,207; health permit to operate $470–$1,000; building permit $800–$15,000 depending on construction valuation; sign permit $300–$1,500. The cost range reflects uncertainty in TI scope and valuation. State and federal registrations (EIN, seller's permit, entity formation, EDD, food safety certs, music licenses) add $570–$3,000 and 1–35 days but are not in the entitlement path. If the concept is part of a formula-retail chain and the Central SoMa SUD's formula-retail prohibition applies, the timeline and cost cannot be estimated because that overlay may prohibit the use outright; confirm at the pre-application meeting.
